episodes.178666: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms erupted during the early to mid afternoon hours due to strong instability. A few of the thunderstorms produced gusty and in some cases damaging winds and large hail.
episodes.178766: Accelerated snowmelt from a near-record snowpack due to above normal temperatures produced high and fast flow on drainages in several counties across the Western Slope. As a result, flooding compromised various low-lying roads and areas. This included some lanes along I-70 west of Fruita, Colorado.
episodes.178988: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed into northwest Arkansas during the evening of the 14th. The strongest storms produced damaging wind gusts.
episodes.179001: Scattered thunderstorms developed in the warmth of the afternoon ahead of a back door cold front that sagged into the lower Ohio Valley from the northeast. The storms occurred under northwest flow aloft on the front side of a 500 mb ridge. Instability was quite strong, reaching 2000 to 3000 J/kg by late afternoon. Deep-layer wind shear was   in the 20 to 30 knot range, which supported some organization of late afternoon and early evening thunderstorms. Isolated damaging wind and a short-lived funnel cloud accompanied the strongest storms.
episodes.179002: A couple thunderstorms acquired supercell characteristics for short periods of time, generally less than an hour. These storms formed over the Ozark foothills and moved slowly east to the Mississippi River delta flatlands before weakening. Large hail up to the size of golf balls accompanied these storms. A well-developed mesocyclone with one of the storms was accompanied by a funnel cloud. The storms formed during the warmth of the afternoon along a slow-moving warm front that was draped across southeast Missouri. Periods of sunshine resulted in moderate instability south of the front, with capes around 2000 J/kg. Backed surface winds near the front, beneath 25 to 30 knots of mid-level westerly flow, supported transient supercell structures.
episodes.179214: Widespread, mostly sub-severe convection, developed on the periphery of a low-pressure center as it traversed across portions of the Ozarks. Localized heavy rainfall across eastern Oklahoma lead to an instance of flash flooding near Seminole, OK.
episodes.179281: A period of showers and thunderstorms from May 11-14th resulted in locally heavy rainfall that pushed portions of the Little Sioux River into minor flood stage. Flooding was largely limited to agricultural land.
episodes.179294: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed across the area with a few reports of trees down across the Florida Big Bend and large hail in Jackson county.
episodes.179295: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed across the area with a few reports of trees down. In addition, a slow moving storm over Thomasville produced numerous reports of flash flooding.
episodes.179310: Isolated to widely scattered storms developed along remnant outflow boundaries on the  afternoon the 15th. Saturated soils from previous rainfall in the week led to flash flooding with the afternoon and evening storms. Minor to moderate river flooding also occurred along the Jacks Fork, Current, and Big Piney rivers along with Roubidoux Creek. A few severe storms occurred and one storm near Fair Grove produced an intermittent EF-0 tornado that impacted homes, trees and outbuildings.
episodes.179627: A stationary frontal boundary extending from northern Missouri to western Kentucky triggered clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms across parts of central Illinois during the late afternoon and evening of May 14th.  Most of the storms were concentrated along a Rushville...to Springfield...to Salem line.  Scattered wind damage and hail as large as golf balls occurred across this area.  In addition, heavy rainfall of 2 to 3 inches led to localized flash flooding.
episodes.180212: A weather system moving through Utah brought widespread precipitation in addition to isolated flash flooding and strong wind gusts.
episodes.180258: Strong winds gusts were generated out of some thunderstorms that were collapsing.
episodes.180366: Thunderstorms with heavy rainfall caused flooding. Rescue crews pulled four people from floodwaters early in the morning after the people fell into quickly rising flood waters. All people were rescued successfully.
episodes.180488: An inverted trough of low pressure over the Bahamas induced a northeast lower tropospheric flow over the Florida Keys.  Combined with ample moisture, convective cloud lines developed repeatedly over the Lower Florida Keys. A few waterspouts were noted throughout the midday and evening hours.
episodes.180702: Showers and thunderstorms developed near a cold front across portions of North and Central Texas. An isolated severe storm produced quarter size hail in Dallas County. Unfortunately, a dad and his son lost their lives due to a lighting strike in the Valley Mills area of Bosque County.
episodes.180705: Four consecutive days of light to heavy rainfall events during the middle of May resulted in near 1.5 inches and some minor flooding along the more narrow, shallow rivers in northeast Iowa. Initial light to moderate rainfall on May 12th quenched soils from a drier than normal spring, while subsequent storms over the weekend of May 13th-14th resulted in rapid runoff and minor flooding along the Little Cedar and Turkey Rivers. Along the Little Cedar River, the highest realized height above flood stage occurred in Nashua (Chickasaw County) on May 16th with 0.94 feet. Along the Turkey River, the river gauge in Cresco (Howard County) crested 0.57 feet above flood stage on May 15th.
episodes.180874: Thunderstorms formed along a mesoscale boundary that moved from the Texas coast into a moist, unstable airmass. One of these storms produced a tornado and damaging wind gusts.
episodes.180938: A prolonged period of well-below-average spring temperatures combined with an above-average winter snowpack created a dynamic breakup of the Yukon River. This resulted in numerous ice jams and snowmelt flooding on the Yukon River. Breakup flooding began on May 12th in eastern Alaska in Eagle and ended on June 3rd in the Yukon River delta at the Bering Sea coast at the community of Emmonak. The primary cause of this active flood year was a 1-2 week delay in breakup when compared to typical timing. April temperatures were well below normal, and when temperatures began to warm in early May, it melted the low-elevation snowpack quickly. Because of the relatively quick addition of snowmelt onto strong ice, the ice was more susceptible to jamming and floods. In addition to the late breakup, the snowpack this winter was 1 to 1.5 times greater than the climatological normal for interior and western Alaska. Significant ice jams and associated flooding on the Yukon River in Canada resulted in large volumes of ice and water to move down the Yukon River into Alaska.
episodes.181002: Another round of strong storms produced heavy rainfall across the area, resulting in flash flooding during the afternoon of May 15.
episodes.181051: A thunderstorm developed in the Florida panhandle and produce a high wind gust.
episodes.181122: Another typical summertime pattern of scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms in the late afternoon was in place for May 15th. A robust thunderstorm complex developed southwest of Lake Pontchartrain in St. James Parish where it produced damaging winds. The complex shortly exited the area across the Atchafalaya River that evening before producing any more damaging winds.
episodes.181130: A weakening upper ridge combined with peak heating led to scattered afternoon thunderstorms across West Tennessee on May 15, 2023. A couple of storms became severe with damaging winds and large hail.
episodes.181213: Rapid snowmelt during a period of unseasonably warm temperatures resulted in a debris flow that washed out a bridge on Spirit Lake Memorial Highway (State Route 504.)  Twelve people visiting Johnson Ridge Observatory were trapped by the blockage and were evacuated by air rescue.
episodes.181564: A lingering warm front as well as remnant outflow boundaries were the triggering mechanisms for storms. Some of the storms produced large hail, damaging winds and flash flooding.
episodes.181835: Some storms developed across the area each of these days which produced an isolated severe storm each day.

events.narrative: Numerous roads were flooded in Ashland.
The Brimstone Reservoir RAWS station recorded a wind gust of 63 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.
Several viaducts and roads were flooded in Springfield.
Water was flowing across parts of Route 125 near Newmansville Road.
A vehicle was stalled in high water west of Divernon.
The Nephi West mesonet station recorded a wind gust of 59 mph as a result of outflow winds associated with a nearby cluster of showers and thunderstorms moving through the area.
A tree was down on a power line.

The Little Sioux River at Spencer, IA rose above flood stage on the morning of May 14 before cresting around 0.89 feet above flood stage (10.89 feet) on May 16th. The river then fell below flood stage on the morning of May 18th.
Thunderstorm wind gusts were measured to 60 mph.
Several roads were underwater in Morrisonville.

The breakup front progressed towards Fort Yukon on May 14th, finally stopping (jamming) just below Fort Yukon by late afternoon/evening. Water levels rose rapidly over bank and resulted in moderate flooding of the community. The river crested the night of the 14th. Several homes/structures were inundated with water. The tribal hall was flooded with water just up to the floor level with likely damage to the floor.  The road to the east of the Tribal Hall was breached to help reduce water levels with water flowing through the breach and back towards the Yukon River. The levee held well and prevented more significant damages. A local observer reported that water levels came to within one foot of overtopping the low spots along the levee, and estimated that the water level was similar to 1981. Water started receding early in the morning of May 15th when the ice jam released. The water took several days to fully drop back within bank.
Station (PANN2) Pancake Raws, Elevation 5165 feet.

Two people trapped by flood waters along with two people who had attempted to help were successfully rescued by the Eastern Douglas County Fire Department and Missouri Highway Patrol after being swept downstream.  No injuries were reported.

Volunteer observers in Howard County reported 0.97 inches of rainfall near Cresco on May 12th as well as minor flooding in low lying areas near Davis Corners on May 14th. As a result of the heavy rain, the Turkey River in Cresco rapidly rose on May 14th, cresting 0.57 feet above minor flood stage of 1128.5 feet above sea level late that night. It then fell below flood stage during the early morning of May 15th.

Significant runoff from heavy rainfall upstream resulted in a rapid rise of water and minor flooding along the Little Cedar River near Orchard on May 15th. Minor flooding was initially realized late on May 14th, with the river cresting 0.51 feet above flood stage of 1081.5 feet above sea level during the early morning of May 15th. It then fell below flood stage later that morning.

The Spirit Lake Outlet Bridge on State Route 504 near milepost 43 was washed out by rock, mud, ice, and water around 9 pm, blocking access to the Johnston Ridge Observatory. Twelve people and one dog were airlifted from one side of the slide to the other as there are no alternate routes. The slide caused power outages in the area.

Significant runoff from heavy rainfall upstream resulted in rapid rises and minor flooding along the Turkey River in Spillville on May 15th. Minor flooding was initially realized the morning of May 15th, with the river cresting 0.48 feet above flood stage of 9.0 feet during the afternoon of May 15th. It then fell below flood stage that evening.
Numerous streets flooded due to heavy rainfall.

Strother Street, east of Main Street, closed due to continued flooding/water across the roadway.

Closures were implemented on the outer lane of I-70 at Skipper Island west of Fruita in both directions as a result of flooding along the Colorado River. The closure was updated to only include the right lane of I-70 westbound several days later.
Trees were knocked down on Allsboro road at Liberty road.
Trees down at the intersection of Allsboro road and Redbud road.
A tree was blown down along Centerville Road.
Weather station recorded 72 mph wind and 7 trees were downed in the city. Pea size hail  was also reported.
N Eldridge Pkway was made impassable due to floodwaters between FM 1960 and Falbrook.
A tree was blown down along Tram Road.
A report of quarter size hail was received via mPING.
Power poles were snapped and at least 12 were blown down from a possible microburst. Several trees were blown down in the same area.
A tree blown down into a residence along CR 51 in Lexington.
Nickle sized hail was reported.
Emergency manager reported one tree down and six utility poles down near the intersection of 3127 and highway 20. Time estimated by radar.

A National Weather Service storm survey determined that an intermittent EF-0 tornado touched down near Fair Grove, Missouri and tracked to the northwest about a mile and a half. Maximum wind speeds were 77 mph with a maximum path width of 75 yards. At the start point of the tornado, a home sustained minor damage to siding., otherwise sporadic and sparse tree damage was noted along the tornadoes path. Just before lifting, several outbuildings suffered significant damage.
A personal weather station measured a wind gust of 61 mph.
A father and his son were struck by lightning walking home from the bus stop. The father died the same day but the son died weeks later, in June.
A thunderstorm produced wind gusts measured at 50 kts by the ASOS at the South Texas Regional Airport in Hondo.
Golf ball sized hail was reported. Time was estimated from radar.
Hail around golf ball size was reported on social media near Alford.
A power line and tree were blown down across the road on Tennessee Street in Alford.
A thunderstorm produced a funnel cloud near I-35 and FM 117 in Dilley. The Frio County Emergency Manager relayed a video of the funnel cloud to our office.
Trees were reported blown over and swings flipped over at this location. Time was estimated from radar.
The intersection of Highway 65 and Stockwood Road were impassable due to high water at a low water area.

An NWS Storm Survey found that an EF-0 tornado initially touched down on the west side of Dilley where damage to hardwood trees was noted. The tornado then moved in a northeasterly direction, causing damage to roofs of buildings on either side of I-35. The |tornado lifted on the east side of the interstate and covered approximately 0.7 miles over a span of 2 minutes. Maximum winds were estimated at 75 mph.
Quarter-size hail was reported in a swath from around Williamsville to just south of Greenville.
A funnel cloud was reported in southern Wayne County, between Williamsville and U.S. Highway 67 south of Greenville.
A pine tree was blown down along with some roof damage and a broken flag pole in the Hilton area.
Golf ball size hail fell in the Leora area, about 9 miles northwest of Bloomfield.
Route CC was closed due to flooding of a low water area.
Several trees were uprooted or snapped in Trenton. At least one home was damaged by a downed tree.
